points.description: 23 October: students and workers demonstrated in Budapest; Stalin's statue pulled down; secret police fired.
Nagy became Prime Minister; Soviet troops withdrew from Budapest.
Nagy promised free elections and other freedoms, and on 1 November announced withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: On 23 October 1956 students and workers demonstrated in Budapest, pulled down the statue of Stalin and fought the secret police after it fired on them. Nagy became Prime Minister and Soviet troops withdrew from the city. Nagy promised free elections and other freedoms, and on 1 November announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact. On 4 November Soviet forces returned, attacked Budapest and crushed the rising, and Kádár was installed as leader.

stem: Explain why the USSR invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968.

points.description: Identifies fear that the reforms would spread.
Explains that leaders in the USSR, East Germany and Poland feared their own people would demand the same freedoms.
Identifies the end of censorship / loss of party control.
Explains that free discussion threatened the Communist Party's monopoly of power and might eventually threaten Warsaw Pact unity.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Brezhnev feared that the Prague Spring would spread: the leaders of East Germany and Poland in particular warned that their own people would demand the same freedoms. With censorship ended, critics could openly attack the Communist Party, and the USSR feared that the party would lose its monopoly of power and that Czechoslovakia might eventually drift away from the Warsaw Pact, even though Dubček promised to stay.

hints: Dubček stayed in the Pact, so the fear was something else.

stem: Explain why there was opposition to Soviet control in Hungary in 1956.

points.description: Identifies the harsh rule of Rákosi and the secret police.
Explains that arrests and fear made the regime hated.
Identifies poverty and Soviet economic exploitation.
Explains that low living standards were blamed on unfair trade with the USSR.
Identifies de-Stalinisation (Secret Speech; Poland's reforms).
Explains that this gave Hungarians hope that the USSR would accept change.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Hungarians hated the Stalinist rule of Rákosi, whose secret police imprisoned thousands and created fear. Living standards were low, and many blamed the USSR for taking Hungarian goods and resources on unfair terms. Catholic and nationalist feeling also made many resent communist and Soviet control. The trigger was de-Stalinisation: Khrushchev's Secret Speech of February 1956, the removal of Rákosi and the reforms in Poland gave Hungarians hope that the USSR would now accept change.

hints: Long-term grievances and a short-term trigger.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a statement of the kind broadcast by Soviet radio in August 1968 (invented for this question)

> At the request of loyal Czechoslovak communists, the fraternal armies of the socialist countries have come to defend socialism against counter-revolutionaries backed by West German imperialists. The Czechoslovak people will thank their friends for protecting their freedom.

**Source B** — a description in words of a photograph of the kind taken in Prague in August 1968 (described in words; invented for this question)

> A young man stands in front of a tank, his arms spread wide. Around him a crowd holds Czechoslovak flags. On the side of the tank someone has painted, in Russian, the words "Go home". The soldiers on the tank look young and uncertain.

parts.label: (a)

To stop counter-revolutionaries supported by the West.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far does Source B challenge the claims of Source A?

points.description: Challenge: the crowd and the 'Go home' slogan show the invasion was not welcomed.
Challenge: ordinary people, not Western agents, are resisting.

Judgement on how far.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How reliable is Source A as an explanation of why Czechoslovakia was invaded?

points.description: Provenance: Soviet state radio, propaganda justifying the invasion to its audience.
Own knowledge: Dubček was a communist and promised to stay in the Warsaw Pact; no Western plot was shown.
Own knowledge: the real fear was reform spreading (East Germany, Poland).
Some truth: some hard-liners did want intervention / the Brezhnev Doctrine expressed real Soviet thinking.
Contradicted by the non-violent resistance shown in Source B.
Supported judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A comes from Soviet state radio, so its purpose was to justify the invasion to its listeners; it calls the invading armies 'fraternal' and claims the people will thank them. My own knowledge shows that much of this is unreliable. Dubček was a communist who promised to stay in the Warsaw Pact, and there was no evidence of a Western plot. Source B, showing crowds telling the soldiers to go home, and the widespread non-violent resistance I know about, contradict the claim that the invasion was welcome. However, the source does reflect real Soviet thinking: some hard-line Czechoslovak communists did want intervention, and the claim to be defending socialism became the Brezhnev Doctrine. So it is reliable as evidence of how the USSR justified the invasion, but not as an accurate explanation of why it happened, which was fear that reform would spread.

parts.explanation: Provenance and content against own knowledge.

hints: Who would broadcast Source A, and why?

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The two crises were similar in their causes. In both countries people resented Soviet control, the secret police and low living standards, and both reform movements were led by communists hoping for a more open system. The outcomes were also similar: Soviet-led forces restored control, the reformer was replaced by a leader loyal to Moscow (Kádár, then Husák), and the West protested but did nothing.

However, there were important differences. Nagy went further: he promised free elections and announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact, while Dubček insisted that Czechoslovakia would stay communist and in the Pact. Hungarians fought the Soviet army, and about 2,500 were killed; in 1968 resistance was mainly non-violent. Nagy was executed, while Dubček was demoted and survived.

Overall the crises were similar in cause and result, but different in aims and methods. The differences explain why 1956 was far bloodier, while the similarities show that in both cases the USSR would not allow a satellite to choose its own path.

parts.explanation: Levels: both similarities and differences with a judgement for the top level.
